## Active

### D-363 — blong-kustomize runs with no database and no framework business realms

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The kustomize realm must run on a bare cluster, so it does not reuse blong-server and does not load
the blong-login, blong-core or blong-access framework realms, all of which are DB-backed. The
framework auto-loads those realms only when the package manifest declares them, so the constraint is
enforced by not listing them in package.json and by removing them from index.ts and browser-test.ts.
Its own orchestrator will implement the model methods against the k8s adapter instead of the db
destination.

### D-364 — blong-kustomize gates its orchestrator layer to the k8s intent

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The generator port lives at orchestrator/kustomize.ts and orchestrator/layer.server.ts declares
layer({k8s: true}), so the layer loads only under the k8s intent and the kustomize namespace is
never registered inside a serving suite. A custom top-level k8s/ layer folder was abandoned because
the framework never loads one (F-361). The plan and handler group sit in orchestrator/generate/, and
the pure planner is the realm-root plan.ts, which is outside every layer folder so it is not scanned
as a handler group.

### D-365 — a component contributes Kubernetes resources through its activation k8s block

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

blong-kustomize collects per-component Kubernetes contributions from the activation.k8s keys the
framework already merges per active intent: k8sReplicas, k8sResources, k8sPorts, k8sIngresses,
k8sEnv, k8sManifests. This replaced the descriptor file the plan first proposed, because co-locating
the contribution in the layer file leaves one place to edit. Objects deep-merge across the realms
sharing a deployment and arrays concatenate; an ingress with no serviceName binds to the Service of
the deployment that owns the contributing realm.

### D-367 — SuiteVolume auto-selects its backend and OpenEBS is opt-in

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

resolveSuiteVolume keeps the default backend at nodeLocal because a bare cluster has no
ReadWriteMany StorageClass; a suite that names a storage class or an RWX provider resolves to
shared. rwxProvider openebs defaults the class to openebs-rwx, and rwxManifest emits
storage/kustomization.yaml referencing the operator manifest as a kustomize remote resource so a
single apply installs it; without a manifest the installer stays dependency-free. The artifact
source is url for the cluster and path for local dev, and retention is carried as blong.io/retention
and blong.io/suite-version labels, with pruning left to the operator because only it has cluster
access.

### D-368 — the kustomize dispatch port serves both the k8s generator and the read API

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

orchestrator/kustomize.ts loads in every intent and attaches the generate and deployment handler
groups; the k8s activation block sets generateManifests: true and start() writes the tree only when
that flag is set, so a serving process never generates. The server-side orchestrator/subject/init.ts
was removed because it declared the kustomize namespace for the blong-server subject orchestrator,
which this realm deliberately does not load; the realm port owns that namespace now. The
browser-side subject namespace file stays because the portal needs it.

### D-369 — images reach the k3d cluster through podman and ctr, not k3d image import

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The dev cluster runs on podman, so its nodes are podman containers and docker is absent. k3d image
import needs the docker API, so the working path is podman build, re-tag to
`docker.io/library/<name>:<tag>` so the kubelet reference matches, podman save to a tar, podman cp
the tar into each node, and ctr -n k8s.io images import inside the node. Importing into every node
matters because a DaemonSet schedules one pod per node and the kubelet pulls locally unless a
registry is configured.

### D-370 — the deployment UI is exposed with cluster-level auth, not a login realm

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The realm generates a gateway Service and a UI Ingress whose auth is the ingress controller
annotations: basic auth from a Secret, or an oauth2 proxy auth-url. A UI exposed with no auth block
is a deliberate and visible choice in the suite config. This keeps the realm free of a user table
and of blong-login and blong-access, which need a database, and leaves authentication to
infrastructure the operator already owns. The RBAC Role was widened to read the kinds the UI lists,
namely pods, services, endpoints, deployments, daemonsets, replicasets and ingresses, and nothing
more.

### D-371 — the CRD ships with the suite tree, and a dry run cannot prove the CR

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The BlongDeployment CRD is emitted with the suite tree rather than installed once per cluster, so a
suite can be handed to an operator by the same kubectl apply -k that deploys it. A real kubectl
apply orders CustomResourceDefinition before custom resources, so the CR follows the CRD it depends
on; a server dry run installs nothing, so the CR reports no matches for kind BlongDeployment while
the CRD itself validates. That error in a dry run is expected and is not a manifest problem.

### D-372 — Reconcile applies only the kinds the adapter names, fingerprint-gated

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator applies a resource only when RESOURCE_TYPE_BY_KIND names a resource type for its kind;
the namespace, the CRD, the ServiceAccount and the custom resource itself are reported as skipped
with a reason. Deletion needs a second word on top of apply: apply converges, prune removes. Whether
an object differs is decided by a blong.io/spec-hash label the generator stamps on each manifest,
not by comparing specs: the API server adds defaults to almost every stored object, so a spec
comparison would report a difference forever and re-apply in a loop.

### D-373 — Two cluster identities: read-only UI role, writing operator role

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The RBAC generated in Phase 8b is read-only and belongs to the UI. The apply half needs write verbs,
so it will get its own ServiceAccount, Role and ClusterRole rather than widening the UI role: the
read path and the converge path are different trust levels, and a UI that can only look cannot
damage a cluster if it is exposed through an Ingress. Not yet implemented.

### D-375 — The kustomize UI authenticates against the cluster, not a Blong login realm

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Chosen with the user on 2026-10-05 over loading blong-login plus blong-access-mock: the cluster
already holds the identities, and a second user store would be a second source of truth. The portal
login form takes a service-account token in the password field; the realm validates it with a
Kubernetes TokenReview and then asks a SubjectAccessReview whether that identity may reconcile. The
service-account name is pre-filled or not asked for, because the token is the credential. The form
gains a help affordance revealing kubectl create token and the token field of a
service-account-token Secret. The k8s adapter cannot reach authentication.k8s.io or
authorization.k8s.io yet, so that gap has to close first.

### D-376 — The kustomize UI logs in with a service-account token the cluster verifies

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The portal refuses to render a page without a token, so the realm answers login.token.create itself
instead of loading blong-login, which brings a user store this realm has no database for. The
password field carries a Kubernetes service-account token; a TokenReview says whose it is and a
SubjectAccessReview says whether that identity may create the suite's custom resource, and the
form's username is ignored because the review is what names the caller. The token that comes back is
the one presented: minting a second credential would add a second expiry for no gain. Recorded
openly is what this does not do: the gateway's methods run as the process's own service account, so
reads are protected by the Ingress and the process RBAC rather than by the caller's token. The tree
therefore owes the UI service account permission to create the two reviews, which is what
system:auth-delegator grants.

### D-377 — Port config path is realm.port.property: rename the kustomize port to deploy

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A port is handed only `mergedConfig[realm][port]`, so its config path is `<realm>.<port>.<property>`
and an override addressed one level too shallow is dropped in silence. With the port named after its
realm, that path read `kustomize.kustomize.outputDir`, which looks like a mistake, so
`orchestrator/kustomize.ts` was renamed to `orchestrator/deploy.ts`. The port id is now
`kustomize.deploy`; the handler namespace stays `kustomize` because the activation sets it, so no
handler wire name changed. Renaming again — for example to `plan`, `tree` or `suite` — touches only
the file name, the config path and the docs.

### D-379 — A CR names what a tenant may change, the config keeps the rest

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A reconcile pass derives its plan from the CR, and a CR can only carry what a tenant is allowed to
decide: the suite, the version, the framework image, the profile, the volume, the external services,
the UI, the entry and the intents. Everything else — whether the tree ships the CRD, whether it
ships an operator — is the installers decision and stays with the config the process loaded. The
consequence is a rule about where a suite writes those settings: they belong in the default block,
not under the k8s block that generates the tree, because the operator is a serving process that runs
the microservice intent and re-derives the same plan. A setting that lives only under k8s is
invisible to the operator, and the pass then reports objects it does not manage as obsolete.

### D-380 — The operator is granted rights per tenant, in writing

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

One operator serves every suite the cluster declares, so it reads BlongDeployments cluster-wide, but
it must not write cluster-wide: a tenant that wants a suite grants the operators ServiceAccount a
Role and RoleBinding in its own namespace, and the documentation owes a pair of objects to copy and
paste rather than a paragraph. The generated Role stays what it is, scoped to the namespace the
operator is installed in, so installing an operator never widens privileges by itself. Chosen over a
ClusterRole with namespaced write verbs, which would have been the smallest change to run and the
widest blast radius, and over one operator per namespace, which would not have needed the question
at all.

### D-381 — The watch runs in a handler, so the port only starts it

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A stream cannot be handed back over the deploy port's request path, where the reply is replaced by
null (T-225, T-227), so the watch lives in kustomize.watch.run and the controller calls it through
the handler proxy, which is a local call. The port keeps its resync interval as the fallback trigger
and starts the handler when controller.watch is on, which is the default whenever the plan comes
from a CR: waiting out an interval for a change someone just applied is the wrong default. The
handler reconciles with the settings the controller was started with, so watch changes when a pass
happens, never what a pass may do, and one watch serves every namespace because a BlongDeployment is
reconciled where it was declared.

### D-382 — The operator reports its phase and its last pass in the CR status

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

kustomize.status.edit writes status through the status subresource with one JSON patch operation,
add on /status, which replaces the member whether or not it exists; the CRD declares every field the
status holds, so naming them all costs nothing. The phase is Failed when a step failed, Ready when
every Deployment the plan wants reports an available replica, and Progressing otherwise, and it is
written only by a pass that could have changed the cluster, because a read-only pass claims nothing.
The counts travel as lastResult so a reader can tell a stale status from a fresh one, and the write
is answered rather than thrown: the work it describes is already done, and a pass should not fail
because it could not describe itself.

### D-383 — The rights objects are install-owned, not reconciled

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The first pass from the pod died on clusterroles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io is forbidden for the
ServiceAccount it runs as: the plan carries the Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole and
ClusterRoleBinding the operator runs with, and the reconcile tried to apply them. They joined
INSTALL_OWNED_KINDS beside the CRD and the ServiceAccount, because reconciling the objects that
grant the operator its rights would let it widen them, and the cluster refuses it anyway. The
managed set drops to the workloads it owns — ten objects — and a change to those rights now needs
the install, which is also exactly what a second tenant copies.

### D-384 — The watch ignores the status churn it causes itself

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Writing the status modifies the CR the watch follows, so watching every change made the loop wake on
its own report: the first in-cluster run reconciled five times in a second. The watch now tracks
each CR metadata.generation and triggers only when it moves, which is the standard spec-change
signal and the only change a pass exists to answer; a CR the list did not carry is new and is
triggered without a comparison. Measured after the fix: two passes in seventy-five seconds, one per
renewal, which is the resync.

### D-386 — A retry is a new Job, not the removal of the failed one

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Schema and seed Jobs are named per suite version, and a retry gets a new name rather than deleting
the failed Job. A Job spec is immutable, so D-378 solved the refused re-apply by removing the failed
one, which also erased the logs of the failure that caused the retry; naming solves the same problem
and keeps the evidence. The pass looks for the current attempt, the failed one stays for inspection,
and retention keeps three attempts per version, failures included, labelled after the volumes and
pruned by the operator.

### D-387 — One Ingress per host, named after the host

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

An Ingress is grouped by host rather than by deployment: named after the host as a DNS label
(ui-example-test for ui.example.test), carrying every path that host serves, the UI at its
configured path and a webhook at its prefix. A host is what a certificate and a DNS record belong
to, so it is the unit to group by, and a suffix like -ui names the one thing the object is not,
since it can front a webhook or an API just as well.

### D-388 — One statically named operator per cluster

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator is one blong-operator Deployment in a fixed namespace for the whole cluster, not one
per suite as the tree emits today: a cluster-scoped ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for the CR
and its status, and a Role with its RoleBinding per tenant, which is the pair the RBAC section
already documents for a second tenant. The code was already written this way, the watch being
cluster-wide, so only the manifests move. Static names are the point: a suite name in an object name
is what forces discovery before automation.

### D-389 — A group profile is a map of selectors, not a naming convention

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The group deployment profile takes a groups map in the suite deploy config, each entry a
comma-separated list of realm.layer selectors, so a group is written in the vocabulary the planner
already speaks and a realm named by no group keeps its own deployment. That is what separates group
from custom: there the unlisted selectors still get grouped, here everything has to be listed. A
profile name the planner does not know must fail loudly rather than fall through to monolith, which
is what happens today.

### D-393 — The explicit profile map is group, and custom goes with it

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The deployment profiles end up as four names: namespace, realm as the default, group and monolith.
custom is not a fifth, because the map it takes is the map group takes, so the case in the planner
is renamed and its services key becomes groups in the suite config, in the CRD schema and in the
prose. Keeping both would mean two spellings of one idea and a reader wondering which one the map
belongs to; the map decides the grouping on its own, with no implicit per-realm fallback, which is
what makes the single name honest.

### D-394 — Selectors moved from name to instance, labels to the standard meanings

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The tree's labels now carry the standard meanings: name is the application, which here is the suite,
version is the suite version, instance is one deployment, part-of is the suite and managed-by is
blong-kustomize. That forced every selector off name, which was the deployment, the namespace
Service, the http Service, the operator, the seed and migration Jobs and the cache DaemonSet, and
onto instance plus part-of, because a label that names the application cannot also pick out one of
its processes the moment a second deployment exists. Two costs came with it: changing a selector
replaces each pod once, so it had to land before the release pipeline is trusted, and every object's
blong.io/spec-hash changes, so the next apply patches the objects it owns instead of leaving them
alone.

### D-395 — The operator loads the target suite, it does not hold it

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The kustomize realm is a generator that loads a suite and does not start it: point Blong at any
suite's entry point and it derives that suite's kustomization tree, writes it and exits, which is
what the k8s intent already does. The controller half does not follow that model yet:
kustomizeReconcileRun.ts:235 computes its plan with planFromRegistry(registryView(self.registry),
options), so the pass assumes the operator's own loaded registry is the suite being deployed, and
the CR contributes only options. That assumption is true only when the operator runs from the
deployed suite's own artifact, which is why the tree emits one operator per suite today, and it is
also visible in the manifest, whose Deployment mounts that same suite volume read-only. One operator
per cluster becomes correct once the pass takes its plan from a load of the target suite's artifact
instead: a short-lived child process per CR, one running the k8s intent on that suite's entry, with
the artifact named by the CR's spec.suiteVolume.artifact, fetched by URL or read from a mounted
path. A second in-process load is the wrong route, because one process would then hold two
registries, one log, one cluster service and one exit policy. The consequence for the tree is that
it stops emitting the operator altogether: the operator is installed once per cluster, so the tree
carries the CRD and the CR and nothing of the operator.

### D-396 — The operator applies the tree, the child only generates

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The per-CR child process loads the target suite and writes its kustomization tree, and the operator
applies it, so the child never talks to the cluster and needs no ServiceAccount of its own. The RBAC
consequence is the one Q1 described: a Role and RoleBinding per tenant namespace bound to the single
operator ServiceAccount, granting exactly the kinds the tree carries, plus one cluster-scoped
ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for the CR and its status. One detail follows from the tree
itself: it contains the namespace object, so the ClusterRole also has to allow creating that
namespace, or the apply skips it and onboarding creates it instead.

### D-397 — The operator install tree is generated by the realm itself

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator Deployment, its ServiceAccount and RBAC and the CRD are generated by the kustomize
realm from a kustomize-only entry beside it, so no new package is needed and the realm dogfoods its
own generator. The install tree is committed beside the realm and applied once per cluster, while a
suite tree stops carrying any of it and keeps only the CR. A separate suite package would have added
a pipeline for a manifest set the realm can already emit.

### D-398 — The operator fetches tenant artifacts by URL and caches them

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A CR names its artifact in spec.suiteVolume.artifact, and the operator fetches a url into a cache
directory on a PVC keyed by suite and version, falling back to a path when the artifact is local to
a node. The cache is what makes the same pass work on a watch event and on the interval, and the
fallback keeps the local path form working for a runbook that unpacks the artifact by hand.

### D-399 — Profiles: realm is the default and namespace is the finest split

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

After the rework the default profile is realm, one deployment per realm, and the names are
namespace, realm, group and monolith: namespace splits one deployment per orchestrator namespace,
group takes the explicit map of deployment name to realm.layer selectors, monolith puts everything
in one process, and layer and custom are gone. The default moving from monolith to realm is
deliberate, and the snapshots carry the old shape, so they move in the same change as the code.

### D-400 — The operator keeps three Job attempts per suite version

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Schema and seed Jobs are pruned by the operator, which keeps three attempts per suite version,
failures included, on the same value the volumes use (suiteVolume.retention). A failed attempt stays
for inspection instead of being removed, which is what lets a retry be a new Job under a new name,
and the retained attempts become the history a failed deploy is read from.

### D-401 — The deployment UI bundle ships inside the artifact

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The built UI bundle is part of the published artifact and is served by the suite own gateway under
the static prefix, so one artifact carries both the processes and the UI they expose and there is
nothing else to publish. Building it stays in CI, and authentication stays where it is today, at the
Ingress in front.

### D-402 — A realm role decides what it is in a deployment

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Every deployment question now starts from a realm role: service becomes a process of its own and
owns the namespaces its orchestrators answer for, companion is carried by every process and owns
none, both is carried everywhere and also owns a process, and none is not deployed at all. A realm
declares its role in its own activation k8s block, which is the self-contained-components rule the
rest of the realm follows, and the suite deploy config can override it for realms that do not
declare one yet. An unknown realm is a service, so a new realm is deployed without anyone
remembering to say so. The suite config names srv as a companion because the DB adapter and subject
orchestrator pair repeats in every microservice, core and access as both because a library realm
must be in-process everywhere and still own the namespace the admin API is reached through, and
codec, blong and kustomize as none.

### D-403 — A namespace Service is only published for a deployable realm

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A Service is published for the namespaces of a realm whose role is service or both, never for a
companion, because a companion is in every process and a Service naming an owner chosen from several
deployments that can all answer the call would be arbitrary. That is what makes IService.deployment
a real owner, and it is the other half of why core and access are both rather than companion: they
have to own the namespace the front end reaches, while every other process carries a copy so calls
into them resolve in-process. One shared namespace is deliberate: the subject namespace is
contributed by srv and reached in-process everywhere, so its Service exists for a caller that lacks
the handlers and is otherwise unused.

### D-404 — A namespace is attributed to a realm by name

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A Service is published for a namespace only when a deployable realm owns it, and the owner is
decided from the namespace name rather than from the port that declares it: a shared orchestrator
declares the namespaces of every realm it carries, so srv.subject answers for subject, access and
marine at once, and reading the owner off that port pointed the access Service at whichever realm
loaded the port. The owner is then the realm own process, taken from the profile split and not from
the first deployment that includes the realm, because a companion and a both realm are carried by
every process: asking that question resolved access to the core deployment. A namespace that only
companions declare publishes nothing, and one a profile deliberately left out, as a group map does,
is skipped instead of redirected to an arbitrary deployment.

### D-405 — A port id names a realm by its child, a group by its realm

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The same realm is spelled two ways in one registry: a port id uses the name of the child that loaded
it (srv.subject, where the suite child is called srv) while a handler group uses the realm own name
(server.orchestrator, where the framework realm is registered as server). Anything keyed by realm
has to pick one spelling and say which: the role map and the plan selectors use the realm spelling,
which is why the suite config declares server as the companion and not srv, and why a role declared
on a port has to be looked up under the port spelling. This mismatch is what made the first owner
rule look reasonable while being wrong.

### D-406 — The k8s intent reads the deployment realm set, and layers travel as args

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The k8s intent plans a deployment, so it now merges the microservice config blocks of the suite and
the realms (activeConfigs in core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts): without it a suite that declares a realm
under microservice only, as every suite here does, planned a tree missing that realm entirely, and
the realm profile tree held access and core while marine and login were absent. Nothing is served
either way, the k8s block still turns the gateway and the RPC server off and re-asserts that after
the merge, but it did expose that a library can require a gateway to exist: blong-login token
library called gateway.config() and died with a TypeError there, so it now treats a missing gateway
as absent public keys. The layer set of a process travels in its container args as one flag per
selector, --realm.layer, rather than in a BLONG_LAYERS environment variable: that is the vocabulary
layer activation already speaks, it is per container rather than per deployment shared, and nothing
in the framework read the variable anyway.

### D-408 — The tree for a CR is written by a child that loads that suite

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A reconcile pass has two origins and they differ in where the tree comes from. From the registry it
plans in-process, because that process is the suite. From a CR it does not: the operator is
installed once and reconciles suites it does not hold, so kustomize.suite.generate fetches the
artifact the CR names (cached per suite and version, D-398), writes the CR spec beside the output
directory, and runs the CLI this process was launched with — the framework binary named by the
process arguments, so the version matches — over the artifact own entry with the k8s intent, passing
the spec file, the output directory and the tenant namespace, which a CR carries in metadata rather
than in spec. The child only writes; the operator reads the tree back and applies it, so the child
never needs cluster access. Two things this cost: the k8s port generates on startup and so had to
read the spec as well, which the first end-to-end run showed by planning a tree with no trace of the
CR in it, and reading a tree back has to parse every file, because a kustomization is an object in
the tree and classifying it by name turned it into text.

### D-409 — One install tree for the operator, bindings in every suite tree

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator is one process per cluster, so its own tree is generated from operator-entry.ts with
install true and carries what a cluster is given once: the blong-system namespace, the claim its
artifact cache sits on, the realm own artifact volume with its prefetch or seed step, the
blong-operator Deployment mounting both, its ServiceAccount with a namespaced Role and RoleBinding,
the cluster-scoped pair for the CR and its status, and the CRD, which is cluster-scoped and so
cannot be shipped by every suite without two suites racing to define it. A suite tree therefore
carries no operator and no CRD at all: what it carries is the bindings the operator is granted in
that suite namespace, bound to the operator ServiceAccount, and its own CR at the root of the tree.
The config switch that used to enable a per-suite operator is gone, because a suite running its own
operator is no longer a shape this realm has. Two naming rules fell out of the same idea: the UI
auth-review role is one object for the cluster while its binding stays per suite, since the rules
are shared and the subject is not, and a document at the root of the tree is not a folder, which the
writer learned when it tried to create a directory where the CR file goes.

### D-410 — Constant names inside a suite namespace, suite names outside it

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A suite tree now repeats constants for everything it puts in its own namespace: the ServiceAccount
blong, the Role and RoleBinding jobs, the cache DaemonSet cache, the Service http and the Secret
ui-auth that the UI's basic authentication points at. Anything cluster-scoped keeps the suite name,
because two suites share a cluster and that is where two instances really do coexist: the CR, the
ClusterRoleBinding for the auth reviews and the namespaces a suite declares. A constant is what
makes an upgrade a patch rather than an add-then-delete, and the price is that every reference to
the name has to move in the same commit. Both trees declare the identity their own pods run as
through treeServiceAccount, because the operator's install tree has no suite identity and a suite
tree has none of the operator's. The cache DaemonSet was deliberately left without the version in
its name: unlike a Job it updates in place, and the version label is what replaces its pods.

### D-411 — release replaces prod, and it is the only block that silences refs

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The framework had a prod block, copied by every deployment that wanted one. It is now release: the
single block uat, staging and production share, so the configuration tested is the configuration
shipped. No alias is kept, and nothing needed one, because no realm or suite declared a prod block
of its own; the four places that named the intent were the framework config, the CLI help, the
concepts and rationale intent documents, and this repository's router instructions. The block also
carries the two switches that make a released stdout quiet: log.cluster.enabled false, which was
already there, and log.refs false, which is new. log.impl is deliberately left unset under release,
so the semantic package is never imported at all: the references it would render are the ones being
suppressed. The refs switch suppresses printing only: JSON mode and the retained store still carry
the references, so a process that prints plainly can still be resolved against by one that does not.

### D-412 — The rc Secrets are named after the file and keyed by its basename

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The two configuration files a cluster can supply are mounted from optional Secrets whose names are
constants, blong-releaserc for the realm-managed one at the developer's own home path and
blong-releaserc-etc for the user-managed one at the system path. Constants work because each file
has one home per namespace and the namespace already separates one suite from another. The mounts
use subPath, so the Secret's key is the file's basename, which is the convention whoever creates the
Secret has to follow; mounting the volume at the file's directory instead would hide everything else
in that directory, and mounting the volume at the file's path would produce a directory in the
file's place. A subPath mount is not updated in place, which is exactly what a file read once at
startup wants; the operator reads the same two files because it runs the realm.

### D-413 — The release rc pair is the existing intent-suffix source

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A released process reads /etc/blong_releaserc and HOME/.blong_releaserc with no release-specific
code at all, because rc appends rc to the name it is given and the framework already calls rc with
blong plus an underscore plus the trailing intent as the suffix. The pair is therefore the same
mechanism as the developer's .blong_devrc, which is what makes the two mounted Secrets a release
override rather than a third place settings can hide. Two wrong readings came before this one and
both are worth remembering: a grep for blongrc and releaserc concluded that nothing in the framework
read an rc file, when the names are composed at the call site and never appear as literals; and the
fix was first written as a third rc call named blong_releaser, which resolves to blong_releaserrc
and is therefore dead code that looks correct. What did need changing is that the intents reach
blong-config through env, so that a released process has release as its trailing intent instead of
the default dev. Two consequences for the release pipeline: release must be passed last for the pair
to be read, and the spec of an intent-suffix source is the framework's existing one, so nobody
should add a source for a name a suffix already produces. rc also captures HOME at module scope, so
a test that points it at a temporary home has to set HOME before the first import that reaches rc;
releaseRc.test.ts is that file and says so.

### D-414 — CRD defaults come from the planner's own constants

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The BlongDeployment CRD now declares real defaults for the five fields a CR may omit: profile realm,
intents the suite defaults, the ui path a slash, the volume backend auto and retention three. Each
is the planner's constant, exported for the CRD to use instead of being written a second time,
because the two mechanisms that read a CR are different and both must agree: the API server fills
the CRD defaults in when a CR is applied to a cluster, and a CR read as a file, which is what the
operator does, has no defaults applied at all and falls back on the planner. A test makes both
shapes of the same declaration and asserts the generated trees are byte-identical, which is stronger
than asserting the values, because it fails the moment one side gains a field the other does not
have. The volume backend also gained the auto value it had always resolved: an omitted backend and
auto mean the same thing, shared when a storage class or a provider is named and nodeLocal
otherwise, and the enum now says so.

### D-415 — The suite version is found, and it is not the framework version

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The standard app.kubernetes.io/version label used to be fed by the same field as the image tag, so
every generated object reported the blong-gogo it was built against as if it were the application,
and changing the framework version silently restated the suite version. The two are now separate:
minFrameworkVersion is the image tag and nothing else, and the label comes from suiteVersion, which
reads suite.version first, then the manifest of the package the generator is running from, then the
manifest beside the plan entry, then the string latest. The first source is the ordinary one, and a
suite gets it from its own package.json: blong-suite's config spelled version 1 while its package
said 1.13.0, which is exactly the repetition this removes. The fallback is what the operator's own
install tree uses, because that tree has no suite config at all and its app is this realm; the
discovery is by package rather than by argument, since argv one is the bin the loader was started
with and not the entry, which cost one detour. Two consequences worth knowing: the artifact path and
the claim name follow the same version, so a suite that starts reporting its package version deploys
into a new version directory rather than reusing the old one, and the snapshot's tree pins a version
in its spec so that bumping this realm's package does not move the snapshot.

### D-416 — F's remaining half is an interface change, deferred to the user

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Two implementation choices inside F item 2 were taken as far as they can go without touching a
published interface: the CRD defaults and the version split are landed and verified, and the
remaining two, dropping spec.suite in favour of metadata.name and moving entry, intents and the
image out of the CR, are recorded as todos with their recommendations rather than applied. The
reason is that both change what a CRD already in a cluster accepts, and the user, who reviews the
interface, was away when they were reached: my instructions say to stop and state the decision when
it is critical and the user cannot answer. The plan's direction is not in question, only its shape,
so whoever picks the work up has the arguments in the todo and can apply them without re-deriving
them.

### D-417 — A deploy Job is named after what it runs, not after the suite

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The seed and migrate Jobs are named suite-step-version-hash now, where the hash covers what the Job
runs: the step, the suite, the version, the image, the framework version, the entry, the intents and
whether the suite has a database. The reason is that a Job spec is immutable, so a changed attempt
cannot be applied over an old one and a different name is how the change arrives. That replaces the
old answer, which was to delete a failed Job so the next one could be created, and which deleted the
evidence with it: a failed attempt now stays for its logs and the retry is simply another object.
The hash is taken over the inputs rather than over the object the Job becomes, because the name is
the hash output and cannot also be an input, and it is deterministic, so regenerating the same plan
produces the same name and an ordinary re-apply is not mistaken for a new attempt. Both Jobs also
carry the same two labels the volumes do, the suite version and the retention count, so one prune
can work from either. The tree's deployer file is named after the Job, so a reader looking for the
object finds it by the name the cluster shows.

### D-418 — A failed Job stays, and older attempts retire by retention

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The pass no longer removes a Job that failed. It used to, because a Job spec is immutable and the
fixed name meant the next attempt could not be created until the old object was gone, which also
deleted the events and logs of the failure it had just reported. The name now carries the attempt,
so a retry is a different object and nothing has to be cleared; what a failed deploy leaves behind
is the evidence it is read from, and flaky behaviour is not erased by the pass that noticed it. The
other half is retirement: an older attempt is obsolete the moment a new one is generated, so Jobs
are not pruned by obsolescence the way other kinds are, and the policy that decides which of them
may go is a pure function beside the pass rather than a handler. It keeps retention minus one of
them, because the current attempt is in the tree and counts, and it reads the retention off the
objects themselves, because a CR-driven pass never sees the plan its tree came from while every
generated object carries the label.

### D-419 — A released suite serves its own UI from its artifact

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The deployment UI needs no second Deployment and no Ingress of its own: the suite's gateway already
serves the API the Ingress points at, and the browser build inside the artifact can be served from
the same process at the prefix the build uses, which is /s in both the vite base and the static
plugin. Two changes made that declarable. The suite names the bundle root in its release block, next
to the entry path that already names where the artifact is mounted, and the static plugin now warns
and mounts nothing when the directory is not there instead of failing to become ready: a realm-only
suite has no browser build, and an API that refuses to start over a page nobody asked for is a worse
failure than a 404, so naming the path is safe before the pipeline that fills it exists. What is
genuinely missing is the build, which belongs to the release pipeline, and the k3d run is where a
real start can be watched for the plugin's warning. Worth knowing about the path: the version in the
plan's versioned form is the host-side view, since inside the process the artifact is already
mounted at its version.

### D-420 — A release announces itself through one seam or the other

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

kustomize.release.notify is the handler a release calls after it publishes an image and an artifact.
It writes a JSON patch to the CR at spec.version and, when the release moved them, at
spec.frameworkImage and spec.suiteVolume.artifact, and to nothing else: the entry, the intents and
the volume belong to the suite and to the tenant, so a release that rewrote them would be editing a
deployment it was not asked to edit. The order of the two seams is the part worth remembering. The
handler asks the GitOps seam first and returns when it pushes, because a cluster whose operator
watches a repository and a cluster whose operator watches a CR must not both be told, or two
operators converge on one suite. gitops.target is therefore the switch, and the answer names which
seam ran rather than only that something succeeded. The handler is unit tested where a cluster is
not needed, which means the assertions are about the shape of the answer and the order of the seams;
the patch itself is exercised where a cluster exists.

### D-421 — One operator replica is the contract, and no lease

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A cluster runs one operator replica and the realm relies on that rather than on leader election. The
pass is idempotent, because it diffs the tree it built against the cluster and applies the
difference, so two passes leave the same cluster; the status write is a merge patch of the whole
status object, so the last of two identical writers leaves the same bytes; and the operator
converges on CR changes rather than on a clock, so a gap while a pod reschedules is tolerated. The
remaining overlap is a rolling update, which briefly runs two pods, and the idempotence is what
answers it. The knob is operator.replicas and resolveSuiteOperator defaults it to one, so a cluster
that raises it is choosing the overlap knowingly. A lease was considered and is recorded rather than
discarded: it would be a coordination.k8s.io Lease in the operator namespace that each replica tries
to hold and renew, with only the holder reconciling, as client-go's leader election does for every
controller. It needs get, create and update on leases, which the operator's ServiceAccount may not
have today, plus a renewal loop whose failure mode stops every replica at once, and a gate around
the pass. That is a real cost to answer a question this pass does not have.

### D-422 — More than one UI, each on its own host and behind its own deployment

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The user accepted option A for the UI host (the suite declares that it has a UI, the tenant names
the host in the CR) with one requirement added: the model must carry more than one hostname, because
a suite may publish more than one portal and each portal is backed by a different deployment. So the
single ISuiteUi holding one host, and the one hardwired gateway Service named http that every UI
path points at, become a list: each entry names its host, its path, its auth and the deployment it
fronts, and the generator emits one Service per portal beside the one Ingress per host it already
emits. This is breaking for the CRD, so it lands together with the profiles rework rather than on
its own, since one migration of the custom resource is cheaper than two. Left open deliberately:
whether two portals differ in content (each its own browser bundle) or only in address, because the
serving side is a gateway config of the whole suite today, so which process serves which bundle is a
separate decision rather than something the generator can settle.

### D-424 — A planning run detaches the database by configuration

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The user's correction of my first fix for T-235, and it was right on both counts. I had put the rule
in the framework adapter: the knex adapter skipped its startup work when the active intents said the
run only plans. The objection is that a framework adapter should not know what k8s means, and the
answer is a config key the owning realm sets: the knex adapter now honours connect: false, and
blong-server declares k8s: {connect: false} for the shared srv.db beside its dev, ci, upgrade and
microservice blocks. That keeps the policy where the knowledge is, lets a realm whose generator
really reads the database override it for the intent instead of working around it, and leaves the
framework with a key rather than an intent name. The refinement the naive version of the suggestion
would have missed: the adapter has to keep loading. plan.ts derives suite.database from the registry
(view.ports.some(port => port.id.endsWith('.db'))), and the tree owes such a suite a migration Job,
so an adapter unloaded for the intent would remove that step in silence. connect: false registers
the port and skips every query, which is why the detached run's tree is byte-identical to one
generated with the db port disabled outright: the plan is unchanged and only the connection is gone.

### D-427 — The attempt name hashes resolved inputs, not optional CR fields

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The second was chosen: migrationArgs already spells the intents out with the defaults applied, so
the argv alone identifies the attempt and the separate intents field was dropped from the hash.
Reconsider only if a CR field that reaches jobName stops being derivable from the argv.

### D-430 — Namespace Services are added beside the realm Services

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Before that lands, the resolver itself needs checking: the failing lookup named rpc-subject, which
ResolutionK8s never builds (it strips the prefix and answers name.namespace.domain), so the
component was not on the kubernetes implementation at all when the Job ran. A Service for the
namespace fixes the second half only if the first half is real.

### D-437 — The registry holds the per-realm config map by reference

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

D-433 recorded what each realm declares about itself in a map and merged a copy of it into the
registry config, which cannot work: a realm loads after the config of the realm whose child it is
has merged, so the copy held the root and nothing else, every realm read as absent, and the planner
quietly placed every realm as a service of its own, including the ones that had declared companion
or none. The map is now handed to the registry by reference through setRealmConfig and read by
describe realmConfig, so a realm that loads later is visible. Found only in a cluster: the realm
tests had no other realm loaded, so a vacuous assertion hid it, and the generated suite tree is what
showed eight deployments instead of four.

### D-441 — The gateway pair travels as an rc document, mounted under the pod home

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The pair now travels as configuration rather than as two variables of the framework own choosing:
the Secret gateway-keys holds one key, config, whose value is an rc document naming gateway.sign,
gateway.encrypt and the same pair under remote.client, and every serving container mounts it as a
directory at /home/node/.config/blong_release/, where rc reads HOME/.config/blong_release/config.
The realm names the Secret and the deployment creates it, kustomize.gatewayKeysEnsure writes the
document, and the generator mounts a directory rather than a subPath file so that a missing Secret
leaves an empty directory instead of a directory sitting where a file is expected. The framework
keeps its fallback: with nothing configured the gateway generates a pair for itself, writes it back
to config and warns.

### D-446 — Third-party service artifacts come from a YAML catalog in the realm

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The third-party service artifacts are generated by blong-kustomize from a catalog rather than
shipped as a parallel set of manifests. A YAML descriptor per service under
`realm/blong-kustomize/services/` names the adapter it serves, the image and version, the storage,
the credentials and the ExternalName, and the descriptors are schema-validated at load. The set
follows the adapters a deployment activates, and the suite config may switch one off but cannot
switch on a service nothing uses. The adapted resources are a kustomize base per service with
overlays for the dev cluster and for a release deployment, published through the plan/spec/generator
path so plans, diffs and prunes carry them. Storage is a PVC whose class comes from config and
credentials are generated into a Secret unless config supplies its own, both overridable. The
hand-written manifests in `test/integration` stay where they are, for the adapter matrix; only the
kustomize-e2e job installs the generated set, which is what proves the generator end to end.
Keycloak's deployment and its plain init Job are owned now, while suite-specific realms, roles and
clients wait for D-433.

### D-447 — The reconcile timer stays a safety net, and the mle block stays as it is

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator's reconcile loop keeps both triggers in every mode: the watch handler remains the event
path, and the interval timer stays as a safety net even while a watch runs, rather than being
skipped in CR mode as it is today. The alternative — making each watch renewal reconcile the CRs it
listed, which would have removed the timer from CR mode and closed T-251's blind spot in the same
stroke — was considered and rejected: a silent failure of the watch should still leave a pass
happening, and the timer is the cheaper guarantee. Two consequences belong to the work rather than
to the decision: the `if (watching) return;` guard in `startController` has to go, and the thing the
safety net actually does is weaker than it sounds, because a nameless pass reconciles only the first
CR in the configured namespace — so the timer should either walk every CR the CRD declares or the
comment should say it is a partial resync. The second item in that review — the repeated key
assignment block in `mle.ts` — is explained rather than changed, because the block is the publisher
and not duplication: `config.sign`/`config.encrypt` take the resolved material so a reader of that
path gets a key rather than a descriptor (T-267, D-441), and `config.public` keeps the public half
under the name MLE clients fetch it by, written from `mle.keys`, which is public-only material. That
is why the route and the login realm, which read the same value through `gateway.config()`, publish
nothing private. A change that derived `public` from the config's own pair instead was tried,
verified on the cluster, and then reverted: an MLE-proxied login against the unchanged framework
answers 200 with a token and no private member, while the change made that answer carry `d` for both
halves. The real gap was a guard, and `core/blong-gogo/src/mle.test.ts` now is it. F-427 records the
misreading that led there.

### D-450 — The operator loop sits beside the watch and its timer is documented

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

`startController` moved from `orchestrator/deploy.ts` to `orchestrator/controller/operatorLoop.ts`,
which puts the file in a handler-group folder. A module there with no default export is reported by
`Watch.ts` as stray source, and one whose default is a bare function is classified as neither
handler nor library and ignored, so the loop carries a default export of itself with a comment
saying why. The interval timer now runs in both modes: the `if (watching) return;` guard is gone
because the interval is the safety net for a change the watch could not see. A nameless pass is a
partial resync, since the reconcile reads the first CR in the tenant namespace — written down rather
than closed, because closing it needs a list the loop cannot take: it has `request` and no adapter.

### D-445 — The build cache is kept one generation deep, pruned by age

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Buildah makes the stage images of a multi-stage build dangling, and that same set is the layer cache
for the next build, so bounding the disk and keeping the build fast pull in opposite directions. The
choice is to keep one generation. The epoch is taken before `podman build`, and the prune afterwards
drops dangling images older than that run: the chain just built stands, the superseded generations
the next build cannot reuse go. Measured on this host, a cold build takes 138 seconds and reports
four cache hits, while the same build run after the retention takes 9 seconds and reports
seventy-two, with `rush install` and `rush deploy` both `Using cache`. The price is one generation
of about 6 GB, in place of the unbounded growth the cache-prune item recorded (F-425). Prune is also
left to protect the layers the live chain still references, so an older intermediate that a cached
step points at remains in the store — that is the retention working, not a leak.

### D-451 — A deploy-time attempt is named after its container, whole

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The attempt name hashes the container the Job runs — image, entry, command line, mounts, resources —
rather than a hand-written list of the plan fields that feed it. The list was missing the resources,
so the first tree that added them could not be applied over the attempt already in the cluster: a
Job template is immutable, and the name is the only way a change reaches a cluster. Hashing the
container makes the two impossible to disagree, because the Job is built from the same value. The
cost is that every existing attempt name changes once, so a cluster runs the migration a second time
under the new name and keeps the old Job as evidence — the shape F-410 already described, and the
reason the doc says what the hash is for.

### D-453 — A watch-executed group pins through one helper with a fallback

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The tree spec now takes its plans from `_fixtures.ts` and pins the configuration each generated
process is given with `assert.snapshot`, and because the dev server watch runner executes this group
without a snapshot context (T-214) the pin goes through one `pin(assert, name, value)` helper that
falls back to asserting the structure was produced. The alternative considered was to implement the
context the runner lacks, and it was refused on a property of the store rather than on effort: TAP
keys a snapshot by the subtest titles the tap run produces, the dev server cannot reproduce those
titles, so a second store would be a second source of truth for the same pins and regenerating one
would not update the other. What that leaves is a step that pins nothing in the watch run, which the
helper says out loud instead of a `typeof` guard repeated at every call, and T-214 stays the item
that closes it. The cost was measured before deciding: restoring the staged store made both pins
fail with Snapshot entry not found, so the pins are load-bearing in the tap run.

### D-454 — Structure is pinned per step, not once at the end of the chain

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The tree spec pins each structure where the step built it, rather than with one `snapshot("*")`
marker at the end of the chain or `group(name, {autoSnapshot: true})`. Three reasons decided it.
Failure attribution: a marker snapshots the accumulated context, so a changed port and a changed Job
name arrive as one diff under one name, while a per-step pin says which structure moved. The
fallback: a marker is a no-op in the runner that has no snapshot context, where `pin` still asserts
the structure was produced (T-214), and `autoSnapshot` would pin the temporary directory every step
returns. And the shape of these steps: `autoSnapshot` is for a group whose steps already return
their values, which these do not — they return a directory handle and assert on their way. The cost
is one name per structure, which is what the assert messages used to carry. Two smaller notes from
the same work: a fixture read out of `lib` is typed `unknown`, so a step that keeps a plan in a
variable says `as IDeploymentPlan` where it is built, the price of injecting values instead of
importing them; and a snapshot publishes what a regex on serialized text hid, since the store now
holds the mount paths and the environment a pod is given.

### D-455 — A registry pass is refused when the process declares no suite entry

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The guard reads `options.entry`, which `planOptionsOf` takes from `config.suite.entry`, because a
registry pass is the statement "reconcile the suite this process is" and a process that declares no
entry has no suite to be: the failing run was this realm own CLI, whose config names no suite at
all, planning its own ports (`blong`, `codec`, `kustomize`) and deploying them into the namespace it
was handed (F-406). The alternatives in the entry were refused for cost rather than for taste:
requiring `--from` explicitly would break the ordinary in-process pass a deployed suite makes, and
narrowing by namespace would not help, because a namespace says where a pass may write and not
whether it has a suite to write. The risk accepted is a suite process whose config omits
`suite.entry` and that reconciles itself from its own registry: it is refused now, and the reason
names the flag to pass. The operator is unaffected, because its passes are CR-origin by
configuration.

### D-456 — The monolith setting rides the profile, on both command lines

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The generator emits `--remote.canSkipSocket=true` for a monolith profile and nothing otherwise, on
the deployment command line and on the migration step, because the setting is a statement about the
deployment shape and the tree is what knows the shape. Emitting it as a flag rather than as a
variable reuses the config path the loader already merges, and it keeps the two command lines equal
in kind: the intents are positional and every flag follows them, so the trailing positional that
names the rc file is still `release` (T-253), and the migration attempt name changes with the flag,
which is what makes a corrected command line a new attempt rather than an immutable Job that has to
be deleted (D-386). The cost is visible in the pinned args: the flag sits between the intents and
the layer selectors.

### D-457 — A service is implied by the adapter kinds a plan activates

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The catalog decides three things, and each was a choice between two defensible shapes. A descriptor
is data under `services/`, validated at load with a closed schema, because a service is added by
adding a file and a misspelled field (`kind` for `kinds`) would otherwise generate nothing and say
nothing. Which services a deployment needs is read from the adapter kinds its ports carry — the
framework own vocabulary (`core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server.ts`: knex, mongodb, redis, kafka,
vault, s3, keycloak, k8s) — rather than declared again in the suite config, because the two would
disagree the first time a realm activated an adapter; the suite may switch one off (it runs its own
installation) and may not switch one on for an adapter nothing activates, which is refused because
the workload would be one nothing dials. And the alias a realm config keeps naming is named after
the service (`mysql`), not after a host, so the workload can move namespace without a configuration
change; that alias is derived, not typed. The database list is read from the connections the plan
ports name, which is the same list the integration matrix init script spells out by hand — one place
that knows a schema name.

### D-458 — The stale subject Service was deleted by hand and the stuck rollouts reverted

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator reported the subject Service obsolete (its spec-hash label is an older tree than the
live one) and deleted nothing, because a CR carries no prune and the pass deletes only when asked.
Deleting it by hand is what a prune pass would have done, and it is not what caused the crash loop.
The four deployments were then restarted to test whether the Service was the cause; all four lost
the same way, and rollout undo put the serving revisions back so the dev cluster stays usable. A
mass restart of a suite on a cold cluster is not a safe way to pick up a new artifact, since the
loading order it exposes is the one that fails.

### D-460 — A service base is a template the plan renders, not a kustomize overlay

> _2026-10-08 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The plan proposed `services/<name>/{base,overlays/{dev,release}}` with kustomize overlays varying
per intent, and the implementation does something narrower: a base is a Kubernetes document with
`${placeholder}` values (namespace, image, claimName, initConfigName, credentialsSecret), and the
generator substitutes what the plan holds for that service before it enters the tree. Overlays were
avoided because the tree is generated per pass and applied with a single `kubectl apply -k`, so
there is no second kustomize layer to read an overlay: the plan is already the per-tenant,
per-intent variation (its storage class, its databases, its namespace, its overrides), and a
placeholder the generator does not know is an error rather than a literal `${image}` reaching a
cluster. The consequence is that a base may not depend on kustomize features at all (no name
prefixes, patches or configMapGenerator references), which is why the generated Service and
ConfigMap are written by the generator beside the base rather than produced by it.

### D-461 — A pass deletes obsolete objects only in the suite's namespace

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The operator reconciles a declaration, and a declaration that stops naming an object has to be able
to remove it — otherwise switching a service off is a promise rather than a fact. The scope is the
suite's namespace and nothing wider: the generated third-party services live in a namespace of their
own precisely so that a config edit cannot take a shared database with it, so the ExternalName
alias, which sits in the suite's namespace because that is where a realm's config dials it, is
deleted when its service is switched off, while the workload, claim and Service beside it are
reported as obsolete and left running for whoever owns that namespace to retire. The consequence of
that boundary is accepted in both directions: an external service a deployment chooses to place in
the suite's own namespace is deleted with everything else there, and prune is a setting of the pass
— on in the operator's Deployment, and available to any caller that asks for it.

### D-462 — A generated service's credentials are written beside the suite as well

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A pod reads only the Secrets of its own namespace, and the alias a generated service publishes is
dialled from the suite's namespace — so a deployment that points at its generated database would
find the name answering and the password unreadable. The tree therefore writes the credentials
Secret twice: once in the service's namespace, where the workload reads it, and once in the suite's
namespace, where the deployment that dials the alias reads the same values. The values are derived
rather than random (suite, namespace, service and key), so the copy is the same on every pass and
needs no syncing: a rotation is a change to the derivation, which both copies follow when the tree
is applied. Only a Secret this realm generates is copied — one a deployment owns is theirs to place,
and this realm has no values to copy. D-461's boundary applies to the copy as well: it lives in the
suite's namespace, so switching the service off deletes it with the alias.

### D-463 — Placement is a typed override, passed through rather than interpreted

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A deployment whose storage binds to one node has to name where a generated workload may run, and the
only place a node selector, a toleration or an affinity can live is the pod spec of the rendered
workload. The realm takes them as a typed placement object on the service override, in Kubernetes'
own shapes, and merges them into the pod spec shallowly — what the deployment names is the last
word, exactly as the labels beside it are stamped. The realm never reads their meaning: a toleration
belongs to the cluster's scheduler, and a realm that validated one would be a second, weaker copy of
the API. The config schema needs no entry, because the port declares additionalProperties and the
value of a service key is unconstrained, so nothing is dropped on the way in. Depth is deliberate: a
nested merge would let a base's affinity and a deployment's silently combine, and no base ships one.

### D-464 — The prune sweeps the kinds a suite can own, whether or not the tree names one

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The pass looked up only the resource types its tree named, which cannot see the object whose kind
left the tree: the credentials copy a switched-off service wrote into the suite's namespace is a
Secret, a tree with no Secret left builds no secret group, and the copy was orphaned by the pass
meant to remove it. So the sweep is the adapter's vocabulary minus the install-owned kinds. The
install-owned ones stay out for the reason they are skipped at apply time: an operator that swept
the Role it runs under could delete its own rights. Version-named objects, those carrying
blong.feasible.one/retention, are kept out of obsolescence pruning too, because their retirement is
a number another step reads.

### D-466 — An init that has to call a server is a Job the deployment writes

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A service that cannot be initialised by a file its workload mounts — Keycloak, whose realms, clients
and users are created by calling a running server — needs a step of its own. Which of the two shapes
a service is stays the descriptor answer (initJob in its values), because that is a fact about the
image rather than a preference; what the step does is the deployment own, supplied verbatim as
init.script in the service config, since this realm has no opinion about what a realm of Keycloak
contains. A deployment script is written as it arrives — no placeholder expansion, because it is not
a template, which is why it is carried apart from the descriptor initScript — and it is mounted and
run as a file rather than quoted into a command line, so what ran can be read back from the cluster.
The Job name carries a digest of the script because a Job spec cannot be changed, and a failed
attempt is left where it is, which is how a failed init is read.

### D-467 — Pods wait for the artifact marker, and the runbook re-fetches before it applies

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Two changes, one contract. Every pod that runs code from the suite volume — the suite Deployments,
the migration Job and the operator Deployment — now carries an init container that waits for
`.blong-artifact-ready`, and the path-source branch of `fetchCommand` writes that marker too,
because a copied tree is as whole as an unpacked one and a reader would otherwise wait forever. The
developer runbook then re-fetches _before_ it applies the tree and restarts only the processes after
it, because the fetch replaces the directory in place and a one-attempt step that started first
loses that race. Rejected: letting the migration Job retry, which hides a race instead of ordering
it; and skipping the re-fetch when the marker is present, which would break the local cycle, where a
rebuilt artifact keeps both its version and its URL.

### D-468 — A new identity means a new directory, so a volume is never rewritten in place

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

This is what the marker gate and the atomic swap were for. A new directory per identity means no
reader can be reading a tree that is being wiped, the notification the prefetch used to give is
gone, and the marker documents a whole directory for the pruner rather than holding a lock. The
`Directory` type on the consumers already keeps their pods Pending until the directory exists, which
is the only ordering the first fill needs.

### D-469 — A volume is identified by the artifact, filled per node

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The identity joins the version to an eight-character stamp taken from the artifact: a `digest` when
the publisher computes one (the runbook hashes the zip it wrote, and a release publishes the same
field) and a `deployedAt` when the caller stamps it, which is what a `path` artifact does instead of
costing a directory walk. It is always an input rather than the clock at generation, because the
operator regenerates the tree on every reconcile pass and a value read then would mint a new volume
and a new migration attempt every thirty seconds.

### D-470 — One Job per node fills the volume and prunes the retired ones

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The cache DaemonSet and its placeholder container are gone: the operator generates one Job per node,
pinned to that node and mounting its hostPath, which fetches into a staging directory, renames it
into place so no reader ever sees a partial tree, and then keeps the newest X directories under the
suite and deletes the rest. The order is the directory listing, because a digest has no recency, and
the retention is read at the fill rather than in the name: lowering it mints nothing and takes
effect the next time a node fills. Pruning at the fill rather than on every pass is the trade: a
pass that fills nothing has nothing new to retire.

### D-471 — Retention is two fields, and an attempt is named after the deploy

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The volume keeps three identities and the migration step keeps five attempts, each with its own
field and label, because the two are unrelated quantities: one is disk on every node and the other
is one Job. The migration attempt is named after the plan deploy stamp rather than after the shape
of its container, so a re-apply of the same artifact is idempotent, a changed artifact mints exactly
one attempt, and lowering the retention never mints one. The plan also carries the node list,
because the fill Jobs are per node: generation stays a pure function of the plan, at the cost of the
committed trees showing the node set their fixture names.

### D-476 — The fill makes the artifact's links relative

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Rush's create-links.js writes absolute links computed from the directory it runs in, which tied the
artifact to one place: a reader had to mount it at the path its links named, which is why the tree
borrowed a second mount of the node root (D-472) and why mounting the artifact at its own identity
path was next on the table (D-474). The owner chose the third way, and the fill now rewrites every
link as a relative one before it publishes the tree — one Node pass over the artifact, in both
commands, before the move in the staged fill. The artifact becomes a self-contained tree that reads
from wherever it is mounted: one mount at /opt/deploy/suite for every backend and identity, no
second mount, no per-deploy mount path, and every suite config that names a path inside the artifact
keeps working unchanged. Two checks made this safe: realpath and node are both in the framework
image, and a scan of a live artifact found no link whose target lies outside it.

### D-475 — The tree is a committed base and a gitignored local overlay

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The owner chose a full split: system/kustomize/base/ is committed, holds nothing node- or
artifact-specific, and therefore changes only when the design does; system/kustomize/local/ sits
beside it, is gitignored, composes the base and carries what a deploy actually needs. The split is
decided by each object's name: one that names the artifact is instantiated from a base template
(D-477), one that carries a value the deploy owns stays in the base with a patch, and the fill
script travels inside the fill Job's template because it reads its settings from the environment, so
it is the same text for every node and needs neither a ConfigMap nor a mount. The result is a base
of 25 files a reviewer can read and an overlay of nine small ones, and the composed tree is
byte-identical to the flat one. It supersedes D-473's question about node names: they no longer
appear in the committed trees, and the same split removes the per-deploy churn of the identity
rewriting twenty files.

### D-477 — The base carries templates the overlay instantiates

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The first split left the whole fill Job, the attempt Jobs and the declaration in the ignored
overlay, which answered the boundary question and not the review one: everything interesting about
those objects was invisible in the repository. They are now split by what a deploy owns. An object
whose _name_ names the artifact — a fill Job per node, an attempt per artifact, a claim per artifact
— cannot be patched into place, because no patch renames an object, so the base carries a template
per kind under base/templates/ with PLACEHOLDER where the deploy's values go, and the overlay one
small kustomization per instance that includes the template, appends the identity through nameSuffix
and patches the values back. An object that carries a _value_ rather than a name stays in the base
as an object: the Deployments and the declaration, each with a patch. The placement is decided by
the name rather than the path, which is the rule itself and also covers a claim that names nothing
(the operator's own artifact cache). The fill script was a ConfigMap for one turn, on the theory
that a shared script needs a shared file; the template is that file, so the script moved into it and
the Job lost a ConfigMap, a volume and a mount — the emitter writes a multi-line string as a block
scalar, so it reads as well in a Job as it did in a ConfigMap.

### D-436 — A CLI declares the layer folders its cli run needs

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The cli intent is named by no entry of WELL_KNOWN_LAYERS, so a package that ships a command declares
which layer folders that command runs with, in the cli block of the realm whose handlers it
dispatches: blong-kustomize names error, adapter and orchestrator, kukum names error and
orchestrator, and the demo text realm names orchestrator alone. Declaring it on the realm rather
than in the CLI options follows D-433 - the realm says what it is - and keeps CliOptions.intents at
its `['cli']` default, which every realm CLI shares. A folder a command has no use for is left out
rather than switched off, and a command that delegates its work to a child process re-running the
framework with the k8s intent names only what its own process loads.

### D-465 — The runbook is a library of handler-shaped steps driven by two thin CLIs

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The k3d scripts are TypeScript now, and the split is what makes them reusable rather than merely
shorter: scripts/lib holds one function per question with the machine passed in as {run, capture,
log}, which is the shape a realm handler takes, and the two entry points hold nothing but the
sequence, the flags and what the run prints. rules.ts is the decisions the shell wrote as grep and
`[[ ]]`, which is the only part a test can hold without a cluster, and it is covered by the
test.script.rules group. The developer cycle calls the runbook in-process instead of starting a
shell that starts the framework twice, and the compile step is node's own type stripping, so there
is no build to keep in step.

### D-486 — The flat tree writer stays; a test holds the split to it

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The flat layout was to be dropped in favour of composing the split with kubectl kustomize, so no
code would maintain it. On reading it, the flat half is four lines over the same
serializeKustomizeTree the split writer already calls (writeKustomizeTree's flat branch and
writeSplitTree both serialize through it), so there is almost no duplicated code to remove, while
the reader is the operator: readKustomizeTree is its half of a generation that happened in another
process and compares the tree's object set with the cluster, which a base with patches cannot
answer. Composing there means the operator runs kubectl, and the framework image ships none, so the
binary would ride along in every realm process. I kept the writer and would pin the invariant
generator.ts states (the two are held together by kubectl kustomize) with a test that renders the
split's local overlay and compares the object set with the flat files. Choosing otherwise is a real
decision: it puts kubectl in the framework image.

### D-488 — Materialize the base in JS rather than running kustomize

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Agreed. If the base is generated in dev or CI and only its overlay in the cluster, the operator
still has to apply and compare objects, and D-395 says it compares them with the cluster — which a
base with patches cannot answer without a composer. The chosen route is to materialize in JS: the
transforms that built the placeholders and the instances (withSuiteVolume, instantiate,
