splitWorkload, splitDeclaration) run the other way, with the plan's values, over the objects the
base holds, so nothing new enters the image and what is committed is what runs. Reading the base
rather than rebuilding it from the plan is the point: it is what makes the deployed design the
committed one. Two checks keep the materializer honest: a round trip against the flat tree, object
for object, and the kustomize compose (T-290), which pins the overlay's own semantics. The
alternative, running kustomize, would put kubectl in the framework image every realm process shares.

### D-490 — The layout default lives in the realm's k8s activation

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Not where I expected: the framework's own intent blocks in core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts are typed to
the framework's components, so a realm key there is a TS2353, and the framework's k8s block says
nothing about a realm's config. The default belongs in the realm itself — k8s: {generateManifests:
true, layout: 'base'} in realm/blong-kustomize/orchestrator/deploy.ts, which is the self-contained
place a component's per-intent config goes, and which reaches every repository that runs a
generation rather than one suite's config. layout is also declared in that port's validation, so a
command line may set it and an undeclared value is no longer dropped in silence. The suite names
nothing now. The generator's own fallback stays flat, for an in-process caller that never activates
the k8s intent: that is the shape the realm's specs read back, and making the fallback base failed
five of them. The operator's child names its layout on both paths for the same reason the fallback
exists: with a shipped base it writes the overlay (local), without one the tree whole (flat) — a
pass applies what the child wrote, so it cannot take a default meant for repositories.

### D-491 — The install tree is swept by the operator's own CR pass

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The tenant's namespace is not the only one that piles up: an operator image is an identity, so every
rollout of the operator writes another fill Job per node into the namespace it is installed in, and
nothing reached them. Chosen instead of a CI or release step: the pass the operator runs anyway,
guarded by prune and by the CR origin, because the namespace is the operator's own and the operator
is the only process that sees it continuously. It never selects by name or by kind — only Jobs that
carry a retention label are candidates — so the install-owned RBAC, Deployment and Service beside
them stay out of reach, which is what keeps D-461's safety argument intact.

### D-492 — A pass's deletes cascade rather than orphan

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A delete that says nothing about propagation leaves the choice to the API server, and for a Job that
meant the pods were orphaned rather than removed: a suite's namespace held 37 pods with no owner
reference against 7 Jobs, so nothing would ever collect them. Every delete the adapter issues now
names Background, which is what kubectl does — the owner goes, the collector takes the dependents,
and the call returns without waiting for them, which matters because these deletes happen inside a
reconcile pass. Foreground was rejected for that last reason and Orphan for the reason above. A
caller that needs another policy can name it in the params; nothing in the suite does.

### D-499 — A pass reads every object where it says it lives

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A pass reads every object where the object says it lives, not where the suite's workloads live. The
live listing is taken once per resource type _and_ namespace, and the replica count behind the phase
is read in the namespace each Deployment names — both derived from the objects the tree wants rather
than from a single 'the suite's namespace' constant. The reason is the shape of a suite: the
ExternalName alias sits in the tenant's namespace, but the service it points at — its workload,
claim, Service, init ConfigMap and credentials Secret — is provisioned in the services namespace,
which every suite on the cluster shares. Reading them in the tenant's namespace made them invisible,
so every pass reported them as `to create` and applied them again, and the claim among them came
back 422 (`spec is immutable after creation`) because a bound claim refuses a PUT — a CR that sat
`Failed` while the suite beside it was healthy, and a phase that could never be `Ready` even without
that, since the service's Deployment was counted as zero replicas for ever. What this does not
change: pruning still reaches only the tenant's namespace (D-461), so switching a service off
reports its workload obsolete and leaves it. A listing that fails — a namespace whose RBAC went with
it (F-461) — is reported as a step and the pass carries on, because what it cannot see should be
named rather than end the pass before it writes a status.

### D-502 — The sweep names what it listed, not only what it decided

> _2026-10-10 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

One info line per pass now names what the sweep listed for every kind the tree no longer names, as
namespace/kind=count, and names any scope whose listing failed. The alternative - report only the
survivors the diff found - cannot tell an object the listing never returned from one that was never
listed, and that is exactly the question the surviving credentials Secret asks (T-317). The price is
one line per pass, accepted because the operator's log is what a reader has next to the artifact,
and because the counts in the CR cannot distinguish the two causes. It also turned out to be the
line that showed how few kinds a pass sweeps at all: only the four nothing in the tree names, since
a kind the tree names in any namespace is scoped by the objects that name it.

### D-504 — A service is a folder beside the base, opted in by the overlay

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A deployment opts a backing service in, and the service is a folder that sits _beside_ the base
rather than inside it (the user's (C), in place of the two options D-503 weighed). The base is
generated as if no service were opted in: it holds no service object, references no service folder,
and names neither the namespace a service runs in nor the operator's rights there - so the base is
applicable on its own and is the same file for every deployment of the suite. Each service is a
folder of its own under `services/` at the tree root, with a kustomization that the overlay includes
when this deployment brings it, and everything that exists only because of the service travels with
it: the workload and its claim, the credentials the two namespaces share, and the alias that reaches
it from the suite's own namespace. The namespace a service runs in and the rights the operator holds
there are shared between services (two may run in one namespace), so they are the overlay's, written
once for a deployment that brings one. The deployment generates a service's resources only when the
service is opted in and the zip carries no kustomization for it, and uses what the zip ships
otherwise: the folder is the suite's to keep and to review, and the generation is for the services
it does not. What makes this reachable is that the overlay is where the opt-in is written down - a
base object is applied by every deployment, which is what made the switch unenforceable and left the
credentials copy behind (T-317).

### D-505 — A service folder holds the suite's values, not a deployment's

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A service folder carries the _suite's_ own values — the suite's name and namespace, the namespace
its services run in, the credentials derived from them — and not a deployment's, because a folder
every deployment of one suite uses can only hold facts that are that suite's. The artifact's base
already says the same thing (a committed namespace file, Deployments with a namespace of their own),
so a second tenant was never able to share an artifact anyway; what a deployment owns is its nodes
and the artifact its volumes hold, and those are what the base's placeholders and patches carry.
T-318 assumed the folder held deploy-owned values, was implemented, and was reverted the same day
because the composition refused it in two ways: a strategic merge patch is matched by the id its own
metadata declares, so a patch cannot retarget a namespace
(`PersistentVolumeClaim.v1/mysql-data.shop-services` targets an object the folder holds as
`mysql-data.PLACEHOLDER-services`), and the credentials are written twice under one name in two
namespaces, so one placeholder collapsed them into one id
(`may not add resource with an already registered id`). Both errors came from the composition test
that T-318's work added, which is kept: it composes base, folder and overlay with kustomize and
compares the object count with the tree.

### D-506 — The base and the service folders carry no namespace

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The base and the service folders carry no namespace, because it belongs to the deployment rather
than to the design: a split's halves are shared by every tenant of a suite, and a base that named
one would deploy them all into the same namespace, which is what R1 asks to avoid. What makes that
work is kustomize's own mechanism and the discovery behind the layout: a parent kustomization's
`namespace:` field is a rewrite that runs over everything a child brought, so an overlay that
declared the suite's namespace would pull a service folder's workload into it and collide the two
Namespace objects. The overlay is therefore a root that names no namespace with two children that
each do, `local/suite/` for the CR's namespace and `local/backing/` for the services namespace, and
the operator — which has no kustomize binary — stamps the same two in `materializeGeneratedTree`,
reading them off those two kustomizations rather than taking a plan argument, because kustomize's
field is what a human's `apply -k` sees. The Namespace objects themselves are the overlay's too:
each is _named_ after what it holds, and a name is the one thing a patch cannot retarget. A stripped
object keeps its fingerprint rather than being re-stamped: the hash covers the object the halves
compose to, the plan the base was generated from carries the namespace the CR names, and a fresh
stamp would leave every stripped object fingerprinting something nobody applies, which kustomize
cannot repair because it adds a namespace without touching a label.

### D-507 — The base ships no BlongDeployment; an example sits beside it

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A `BlongDeployment` is the tenant's act — its `metadata.namespace` is where the suite is deployed,
its `spec.services` is what that tenant brings, its digest is what it fetched — so a base every
deployment of the suite shares can carry none of it. A split writes the declaration to
`example/blongdeployment.yaml` beside the base and no kustomization references it: it is a sample a
tenant copies and edits. The flat layout keeps it at the tree's root, where it is the one-off
`kubectl apply -f` convenience it always was, and both round-trip tests therefore exclude it from
the comparison — flat minus the declaration equals the composed overlay plus the example. The
operator never applied it anyway (`BlongDeployment` is install-owned in `apply.ts`), so nothing that
runs the tree loses an object; what changes is that a repository no longer declares a deployment
nobody asked for.

### D-508 — The aliases are the deployment's, and the copy is the suite's

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The external-services alias now belongs to the deployment, which is what makes R2 true for an
artifact that ships a base: the overlay's suite child writes `external-services/<name>.yaml` from
the plan, and the plan already merged the CR's `externalServices` over the suite's own config, so a
CR that points an alias somewhere else is the copy that is applied. Both aliases travel that way —
the one a realm's config names and the one a generated service publishes — because they are one
thing to whoever resolves the name. Two other objects left the service folder for the same reason
the namespace did: with the namespace stripped, two objects of one kind and name in one
kustomization are one resource id, which kustomize refuses. The alias collided with the workload's
own Service (both named after the service, differing only by namespace) and the credentials copy
collided with the workload's Secret, so the alias moved to the suite child and the copy to
`local/suite/credentials/<name>-credentials.yaml`. The credentials copy is also in the _suite's_
namespace while the folder is stamped with the services one, so the folder could not hold it
correctly even if kustomize allowed it.

### D-509 — Credentials are the CR's, and a generated Secret is this pass's

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The credential semantics the CR declares are decided and not yet implemented. A service takes its
credentials from whichever of three things the deployment says: values in the CR, which are
generated into a Secret beside the workload; the _name_ of a Secret the deployment manages
elsewhere, which is mounted as it stands; or nothing at all, in which case no Secret is written and
the credentials come from one of the mounted configs (`releaserc-home`, `releaserc-site`). Deriving
a Secret from the descriptor is kept only behind an explicit opt-in, because the current default
generates one for every service that has a credentials descriptor (D-462) and the requirement is the
opposite. A generated Secret is dropped when the CR stops specifying the credentials, and only one
_this pass_ generated is removed: it is labelled as generated and the sweep deletes an obsolete
object only when it carries that label, so a Secret in a shared namespace that this deployment did
not write is reported rather than deleted (D-461 stays true for them). The copy in the suite's
namespace is mounted as env vars on the suite's pods, which is the half that makes the credentials
reach the processes that dial the alias.

### D-511 — kubectl is a requirement of the composition steps, not a skip

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The two composition steps no longer skip when `kubectl` is missing: they fail, naming the binary as
a requirement. A skip looked harmless and was not — `kubectl kustomize` is the composer a human's
`kubectl apply -k` runs, so a run without the binary reported a green group while half of the
split's contract went unchecked, which is the failure mode the steps exist to catch and the one
nobody reads a report closely enough to notice. The binary is a requirement of a developer's machine
and of CI rather than an optional extra, so `requireKubectl` asserts it and the message says what to
install. The `BLONG_TEST_APPLY=1` gate on the cluster steps is a different thing and stays: those
write to a live cluster, which is a choice rather than a dependency.

### D-512 — A service base stays static; a shared reference is optional

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A service's base stays static even though whether its credentials exist is a plan fact, and the two
cases are handled in opposite directions for opposite reasons. A base a _deployment's_ answer
depends on — whether the Secret exists at all — is rendered and then has the entries that name it
removed (`credentialsFree`), because every placeholder in a base has to fill and an empty one is a
failure by design: the alternative was making the reference `optional` and filling a name that
resolves to nothing, which would have left a database running with no user and nothing saying so. A
reference the _base_ carries for every deployment — the suite's own `envFrom` onto the credentials
copy — is `optional: true` instead, because the base is shared and a deployment that switches the
service off must still be able to start its pods (R5). The label that makes a generated Secret
removable is on both copies, and the prune reads it: a generated credential in the shared namespace
is the one object a pass may delete outside the tenant's, because it is the only one that would
otherwise be orphaned by a declaration somebody removed (D-461, D-509).

### D-510 — The two-child overlay's composition is guarded by kubectl

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The layout the namespace change forced — a namespace-free overlay root with two namespace-declaring
children — is guarded by composing it with `kubectl` in the realm's own test group, not only by the
JS materializer the operator runs. `aServiceFolderComposesIntoTheObjectsItStandsFor` writes a base
and an overlay for a plan that brings a service, then compares the kustomize render with the tree as
a _set of identities_, where the identity carries the namespace. That is the assertion that fails
when the overlay's root names a namespace, because kustomize applies that field over everything a
child brought: reintroducing the field deliberately failed this step and the static one beside it
(`aTreeThatCarriesTwoNamespacesNamesEachItsOwn`). The binary is a requirement rather than an option,
so a run without it fails instead of passing quietly (D-511). Deliberately not added: a negative
control that pins kustomize's own parent-wins behaviour, because that is a dependency's semantics
rather than an invariant of ours — the layout stays correct if it ever changes — so the pair of a
static shape check and this composition is what the design rests on.

### D-516 — The workload's own credentials Secret: dropped or kept?

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The CI job's last step fails on an expectation the pass no longer meets:
`.github/workflows/kustomize.yaml` asserts that after a service is switched off the workload's own
credentials Secret in the services namespace is still there —
`The workload's own copy is the contrast — it stays where it is` — while the pass takes it back,
which is what R3, D-509 and D-512 say should happen and what the live cluster does: the Secret goes,
the workload, its claim and its Service stay, and they are reported obsolete. The step is the older
duplicate of a contract T-318's own text asked to move into the runbook, written for the D-461 rule
that nothing outside the tenant's namespace is removed, which the credentials decision deliberately
superseded. Two answers are possible. Updating the workflow keeps the decision and removes the
drift, at the cost of one more edit in CI. Keeping the workflow means the realm changes instead — a
generated Secret would have to survive in a shared namespace whenever the workload reading it stays
— and D-509, D-512, the runbook's assertion and the switch-off check would be rewritten to match.
Either way the duplication is worth removing: a contract asserted in two places has now drifted
once, and the workflow's step re-asserts what its own `SERVICE_OFF` run already checks inside the
runbook.

### D-517 — The mirror's merge keys are a narrowed table, and an unlisted list is refused

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The JS materializer mirrors kustomize's strategic merge with a table keyed by the tail of a list's
path (LIST_MERGE_RULES): containers, initContainers, volumes and imagePullSecrets merge on name, a
container's env on name, its volumeMounts on mountPath and its ports on containerPort, and a
Service's ports on port. A list of scalars needs no rule because a strategic merge replaces it, and
a list of maps that no rule names is refused with the path in the message rather than approximated
by the old by-name-else-replace rule, which is what let the two composers differ in silence (F-480,
D-488). The table is narrowed on purpose to the lists a generated object carries, which is why
volumeDevices and the Ingress rules are absent, and the step aListMergesByTheKeyKustomizeGivesIt
holds every entry to kubectl kustomize shape by shape and pins both refusals with the binary's own
answer: the one it merges by devicePath, and the two an Ingress has replaced rather than merged. Two
finds came out of that step and are now part of the rule. A patched list entry moves to the front
rather than keeping the base's position, which the mirror had to copy rather than improve on,
because the composer the operator runs and the composer a human's apply -k runs have to produce the
same object. And a realm that wants an Ingress patch has to add the rule for it, because the binary
answers a patch carrying one by replacing the list.

### D-518 — The artifact fetch is a realm module the container runs, not shell in the image

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The framework image installs curl and unzip for exactly one reason: the fill Job and the operator's
tree fetch both run shell that downloads a zip and unpacks it, so the deploy path depends on two
binaries the runtime does not otherwise need. The realm now owns the whole step in TypeScript
instead. realm/blong-kustomize/fill.ts exports the fill (fetch by url or copy by path, unpack the
zip, run the link script, rewrite absolute links as relative, write the ready marker, stage beside
the target and rename into place, prune the old identities) and, run as a program, does the same
work inside the container, so the operator in-process and the Job in a pod share one implementation
rather than two that drift. The tree carries that module as a ConfigMap the Job mounts and runs with
node, which is the shape the script had for one turn before it was folded into the template (D-477)
and is accepted now because the step is a real program rather than three lines of shell. The zip is
read by the module itself over node:zlib, so nothing new enters the framework image and the
Dockerfile only loses curl, unzip and the comment that excused them. Two shapes were rejected. A
generic fetch command inside blong-gogo would hand the framework a deployer job and put a realm's
semantics in the runtime that realm code is kept out of, and a zip dependency added to the image is
one a mounted module cannot resolve anyway, because its directory has no node_modules above it.

### D-523 — The install owns the page's host, and one process serves the page with its API

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

Confirmed by the user among the three routes D-434 offered. The install tree names the host
blong-operator.test and points it at the operator's gateway, so the tenant-facing address belongs to
the installation rather than to any suite; the operator serves the page and the deployment read API
from one origin, which is what keeps a single Ingress pointed at a single Service. It also settles
where authentication happens: the page logs in with a Kubernetes service-account token that the
cluster verifies with a TokenReview, so the identity is the cluster's rather than a suite's minted
pair (D-376). The alternative the entry weighed and this declines is keeping the operator out of the
request path by having the suite's gateway hold the read handlers — that would put the ClusterRole
somewhere it does not belong, since the operator is what already reads the cluster. Two things this
decision does not claim: the dev cluster has no ingress controller, so the host itself is asserted
in the tree rather than exercised live, and the page still cannot render its content because the
operator does not serve the framework calls the portal makes (F-489, T-324).

### D-525 — The page fails on routing, not on a database hop

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The page still does not render, and what stops it is a routing failure rather than a database hop.
One failing call traced at 17:22:48 with the pod log read immediately after shows the process
logging nothing at all while the browser receives a 500 with an empty body, so no handler of any
component ran. The `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND db` that first looked like a dispatch to a `db`
destination is the realm db adapter dialling the suite database host name `db` while the deny was
spelled so that it missed the realm; with the deny effective that line is gone and the schema call
behaves exactly as before, so it was never evidence about this call. Local-first is the documented
rule — `AdapterBase.handle` looks `findHandler($meta.method)` up before falling back to the imported
`exec` — and `subjectObjectSchema.ts` is present in the deployed tree, so what is left to explain is
how this process resolves the namespace `subject`: the realm port is `srv.subject` while the route
namespace is `subject`, the asymmetry T-238 records. The next step is a `--debug` run reading
`/api/sys/ports` to see which namespaces are routable at all.

### D-527 — The operator authenticates the cluster issuer only

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

This deployment replaces blong-login, so it must say what it does instead of identity. Two settings
do that: `blongLogin: false` stops the gateway from discovering a `blong-login` issuer over HTTP
from a `login` Service, which was the call that dialled `login.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` and
made every authenticated request die as a bare `fetch failed`, and `openId` names the issuer the
token actually has, `https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`, so the framework verifies the
caller against the API server key set rather than against a service this cluster does not run. Both
live in the `remote` slice, because that is the codec own configuration — the first attempt put
`openId` under `gateway` and nothing read it. What is deliberately absent is identity: no token
exchange, no session service. Authentication is what the portal needs, and the cluster is the
authority the login already consults through a `TokenReview`.

### D-529 — The session answers itself here, and the tree grows a file

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A cluster token can carry no enc/sig claim, so the keys a caller's calls are signed with reach the
gateway only if the realm supplies them. The realm does: login.token.create records the handshake
the login call carried in its JWE header, identity.checkInternal hands the pair back as the session
GatewayCodec.session reads, and the identity port answers in the same process that verifies the
token. This needs no login realm, no user store and no cluster round trip, and it leaves the cluster
token as the credential. The cost is that identity.checkInternal is the framework's own hook name
and nothing in the framework declares its contract, so the reply shape is pinned by test.session
rather than by a type. The operator's install tree gains one object, services/identity.yaml, so the
tree count moves from twenty-one files to twenty-two and the fingerprint steps of test.tree.generate
and test.plan.find fail until the committed tree is regenerated (D-1867 records that the fixtures,
the docs and both committed trees are the owner's call).

### D-531 — canSkipSocket stays boolean in the operator entry

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The framework now accepts a regular expression source as well as a boolean, and the operator is the
process that would use it: it serves its own realm, the framework realm subject orchestrator and the
namespaces it answers logins and sessions in, and it has no business resolving anything else
in-process. Written as a pattern that named those namespaces, the same entry run with the k8s intent
to write the install tree failed on EAI_AGAIN rpc-cluster, because the cluster adapter was not in
the list, and the realm CLI failed on Unknown database for the same reason on its own db adapter.
Adding cluster fixed the generator and the CLI then failed differently, which is the signal that the
legs do not resolve the same namespaces and a narrow pattern needs them pinned first. Left true,
with the reason in the comment beside it, and the capability is covered by its own unit test in
core/blong-gogo instead.

### D-532 — The operator own node source is the kubernetes.io/hostname selector

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A serving operator cannot ask the cluster the way a `k8s` run does, because the run that generated
the tree is not the run that reconciles it, so the nodes had to become configuration. The entry
names `{selector: kubernetes.io/hostname}` rather than a list of node names: the label exists on
every node a k3s or k3d cluster has, it survives a cluster being rebuilt, and it needs no edit when
a node is added, where a committed list would be wrong in CI the moment the CI cluster renames a
node. A tenant that needs fewer nodes narrows the selector, or names them outright, in its CR.

### D-533 — The session token is signed in-realm with node:crypto, not with jose

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A JWT is a protocol and the repository prefers a library for one, but this realm has no dependency
of its own by design (`kustomizeGatewayKeysEnsure` says why: a key generator is not a protocol
implementation) and the token is one algorithm on one key the realm already generates — P-384 ECDSA,
ES384, over the pair in its own gateway Secret. `crypto.createSign(sha384)` with
`dsaEncoding: ieee-p1363` is the one detail that matters, because JWS carries the raw R||S and node
default is the DER shape no verifier accepts. The unit test verifies the signature with the
published public half, which is what the framework will do with it, so the encoding is pinned by a
test rather than by a comment. Adding `jose` to this package remains the alternative if a second
algorithm or a foreign token ever has to be handled.

### D-534 — The cluster page screenshot budget is noise, not a share of the image

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The framework default is `toHaveScreenshot: {maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01}` in `core/blong-browser`,
chosen for pages whose content legitimately moves. On a 1600x900 viewport that is about fourteen
thousand pixels, and the measured difference between a deployment page showing an error dialog over
an empty table and the same page listing a ready Deployment is 12316 pixels — 0.86 percent — so a
baseline that was plainly wrong kept the suite green for a day (F-507). This realm config now
overrides it with `maxDiffPixels: 50`: a page one browser renders on one OS is a deterministic
image, so the only thing left to tolerate is anti-aliasing, and a difference on the page is what the
screenshot exists to show. The volatile cell is handled where it belongs instead of by widening the
budget: the browse spec redacts the `Created` timestamp, which is the helper own mechanism and the
framework replacement convention.

### D-536 — The operator's install tree carries no identity Service

> _2026-10-12 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The identity Service existed because F-494 answered a verified caller's session by publishing the
name back to the operator: a released process resolves a namespace to a Kubernetes Service of that
name, and the framework's session step asked the identity namespace for the handshake the caller's
later calls are decrypted with. It is gone because that step is now answered in the process that
verified the token. The method is kept out of any gateway — the entry names the namespace in
remote.skipGateway, which is the codec's own setting, checked where the routing decision is made —
and the codec's call goes through the resolver, so remote.canSkipSocket decides and this deployment
answers its own handshake. Neither the Service nor the pod label it selected on is written by the
install tree, and the committed base tree and its kustomization lost them too. What proves it is the
cluster rather than the unit suite: with no identity Service anywhere in blong-system the operator
rolls out, the portal logs in, the deployment page lists the suites, the Reconcile action answers
200, and the three-test Playwright cluster spec passes. A suite's tree still generates the namespace
Services its own containers answer for; that is the generic unservedNamespaces path and was not
touched.

### D-514 — Where the switch should filter the artifact's contents

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

A `SERVICE_OFF` run generates its own tree without the switched-off service, and the operator
composes the tree it applies from the published artifact instead: its base, the service folders
shipped beside it, and an overlay written from the declaration. The switch reaches the first and not
the second, so the pass still plans the switched-off service's five objects as creates and fails in
a namespace the declaration no longer names (F-480). Three shapes are possible and the choice is the
user's, because each contradicts something already decided: filtering at materialize time keeps the
artifact a plain revision and leaves the deployment's decision in the operator, where the rest of
the switch already lives; requiring the artifact to be built with the same switch makes the artifact
per deployment, which its identity and its cache are built against (D-468, D-469); regenerating a
switched-off service's folders in the operator rather than copying the artifact's keeps one source
of truth for the service but abandons the rule that a repository's folder is what a reviewer reads.
Blocked behind it, in the switch-off todo: the operator's RBAC in the services namespace does not
survive the switch either.

Resolved: the operator drops a switched-off service's folder when it composes, and the pass lists
the services namespace for generated credentials so the label's exception can take one back.
Implemented in kustomizeSuiteGenerate, materialize and the reconcile scopes; verified by the realm
suite (97/97) and the SERVICE_OFF run.

### D-515 — A services namespace that is gone fails every pass

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The pass lists the namespace a declaration names so it can take back a credential it generated
there, and a namespace that no longer exists answers `forbidden` rather than `not found` — the API
server cannot tell a missing namespace from an unauthorized one. So a deployment that switched every
service off and then lost that namespace reports `unreadable: blong-services/secret` and ends every
pass `1 failed`: the CR reads `Failed` with everything applied, and nothing changes until a service
is switched on again, since the switched-on tree is what writes the Namespace and the operator's
rights in it. Three answers are possible. Reporting it without failing says the deployment is
applied and no object of this suite can be in a namespace that does not exist, so the condition
belongs beside the pass's other observations rather than in its verdict. Keeping it a failure says a
declaration naming a namespace that is not there is a misconfiguration worth showing, at the cost of
a permanent Failed phase on a deployment that is otherwise exactly as declared. Writing the
Namespace unconditionally removes the case entirely — the namespace is the deployment's to own — but
creates an empty one for every suite that brings nothing. The switch-off flow's check depends on the
answer: it asserts the generated credential is taken back, which is only possible while the
namespace exists.

Answered and implemented: the allowance belongs to the cleanup scope only. A scope the pass adds to
find what a declaration stopped generating holds nothing this deployment is declared in, so an
unreadable one is reported with the other listings and does not fail the pass; every other
unreadable scope still fails it, because an object may be in it unseen. Verified live: with the
services namespace deleted under a switched-off declaration the pass logs 'unreadable:
blong-services/secret (Kubernetes Access Forbidden; cleanup only)' and the CR stays Ready with
failures 0, and the rule is pinned in testReconcileScope (unreadableFailures).

### D-542 — The fill module is minified into a committed derived file

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

CI failed on the prose sweep: `fill.ts` is embedded byte-for-byte in the `fill-script` ConfigMap, so
editing a comment in it changed the ConfigMap, the generated tree and the tap snapshot that pins the
tree, and the suite failed on a spec-hash mismatch rather than on anything behavioural. The first
fix was a hand-rolled comment stripper; the user rejected it in favour of an established tool, and
the repository already depends on `@swc/core`, so `scripts/minifyFill.ts` minifies `fill.ts` into
`fill.min.mts`, a committed derived file of 6354 bytes in one line, and the ConfigMap carries those
bytes.

The module a container runs has to be the module the operator imports: one file satisfies both, and
minifying the embedded copy is what keeps the comment churn out of it without inventing a second
source of truth. The decision this replaces stripped comments and kept the layout, which is the same
idea done by hand with worse tools.

Minifying at deploy time was rejected: the framework image and the operator's artifact carry no
minifier, and installing one to strip comments would put a build tool into a runtime container.

`npm run sync-fill-module` writes the derived file, `sync-derived` chains it ahead of the install
tree and the snapshots, and the fill test re-runs the minifier over `fill.ts` and fails when the
committed copy is stale, so a forgotten regeneration is caught in the suite rather than in a
cluster. The price is one committed artefact that a reviewer sees in the diff, which is also what
makes the freshness check possible.

Verified in the k3d dev cluster rather than only locally: the `fill-script` ConfigMap holding the
minified bytes mounts a 6354-byte `/script/fill.mts` that opens with minified code, and a probe pod
that ran it unpacked the artifact and wrote the readiness marker.

### D-543 — The fill module stays a committed file, not a runtime derivation

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · active_

The question was whether `fill.min.mts` can be dropped and derived wherever it is read. It cannot be
derived at the reader: the reader is the running operator, `generator.ts` renders the ConfigMap
while `orchestrator/controller/kustomizeReconcileRun.ts` reconciles a deployment, so deriving there
would put swc into the framework image, which @@D-542 already refuses.

The module also cannot come from the suite volume, because the volume is what the fill Job creates:
the module has to live somewhere that exists before the Job runs, which is why it travels as a
ConfigMap, and a ConfigMap's bytes have to be precomputed.

Deriving it earlier, in whatever builds the suite artifact, does not simplify either: that build
lives outside this repository, so the minifier would have to be added there, and forgetting it would
surface as a missing module in a cluster instead of as a failing suite.

What the committed copy costs is one ignored file. TypeScript does not compile it, because the
package's include is `**/*.ts` and `**/*.tsx` and neither matches `.mts` (the file list confirms
it), and prettier and eslint are told to skip it because it is minified output. The test that
re-runs the minifier over `fill.ts` is what keeps it honest.

The dev cluster shows the shipping: the operator pod runs with this realm unpacked under
`/opt/deploy/suite/realm/blong-kustomize/`, holding `fill.ts`, the fill template and the generated
`fill-script.yaml`, so a committed file beside `artifact.ts` travels with the code that reads it.

### D-378 — A failed step is removed, and an unchanged step is still awaited

> _2026-10-05 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

The reconcile waits on every Job entry it sees, including the ones the diff calls unchanged, because
a Job that failed in an earlier pass is still a step not taken and the process containers after it
read what it should have written. On failure the Job is removed rather than re-applied: a Job spec
is immutable, so an apply of a failed one is rejected for as long as it exists and the reconcile
would fail on the same step forever. Removing it lets the next pass create it clean, and the failure
is still reported in this pass so an operator sees why.

superseded: a failed step is no longer removed, a retry is a new Job under a new name

Superseded by `D-386`.

entry lists realm.layer selectors, so layer granularity is still expressible by whoever wants it,

### D-425 — How a deployed process stops carrying the deployment realm

> _2026-10-06 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

Confirmed in the cluster and NOT decided: a core pod's log carries the kustomize realm's layer
folders and its ports, because blong-suite declares the realm (the k8s run needs it) and the
framework's manifest gate loads a declared realm in every intent, while the realm's layer says
default: true on purpose for the read API the deployment UI was to use. Three ways out, and they are
not equivalent, which is why this is recorded rather than chosen: gate the realm to the k8s and
operator intents in the framework entry (removes the accidental load everywhere, a framework
change), declare the realm none in the suite's realmRoles (a one-line suite change, but the
accidental-load shape stays for the next suite), or decide the UI's backend first and give the
deployment realm a process of its own. The last one is the design question the gate exposes: nothing
else serves that UI today, since the tree publishes no Service for it, so whichever gate lands, the
portal work is incomplete until the backend has an address. Asked of the user, who was away; the
answer is needed before the change, because the first two options differ in what the next suite
inherits and the third changes what a deployment looks like.

Superseded by `T-254`.

Decided by the user: gate it in the framework. The realm list in core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts now
lets a realm name the intents it is meaningful under, and the deployment realm names k8s; a suite

### D-474 — A nodeLocal reader mounts the artifact where the links point

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

D-472 added a second read-only mount of the suite root, and the owner chose to replace it: the
artifact is mounted at its own identity path, so the pod's namespace contains the very path the
fill's absolute links carry and no second mount is needed. The base tree therefore holds a
placeholder path for that volume, and the gitignored overlay patches every workload with the real
one — which is affordable because the identity moves into that overlay anyway (D-475). The shared
backend was never affected: its seed Job mounts the claim at the same path the deployments do, so
the links it writes already name a path a reader has.

Superseded: the artifact's links are rewritten as relative, so a reader no longer has to mount it
where they point.

### D-472 — A nodeLocal reader mounts the artifact root a second time

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

The fill leaves absolute links naming the host path it ran in (F-449), so a nodeLocal reader was
given a second read-only mount of the suite root beside the mount of its own identity. That is the
smallest change that makes the links resolve, and it was chosen while the owner was away because it
reverts in one line and leaves no path in the tree dependent on a per-plan mount path. Two
alternatives were weighed. Filling the artifact _at_ the path its readers mount, in place, was
rejected because it reopens the window the staged-rename design closed: a reader would import a
half-written tree, which is exactly F-448. Making /opt/deploy/suite a per-plan path equal to the
identity and giving up the second mount is the cleaner long-term shape — one mount, links that
resolve by construction — but it moves SUITE_MOUNT, every entry path, the operator entry, the
fixtures, the docs and both committed trees, so it is the owner's call rather than an autonomous
one. A reader can now reach a sibling identity of the suite through the second mount, read-only;
nothing writes through it.

Superseded: with relative links the second mount is unnecessary, and one mount path serves every
backend.

### D-473 — The committed tree carries the dev cluster's node names

> _2026-10-09 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

A nodeLocal fill is one Job per node and each Job pins `nodeName` to the node whose hostPath it
fills, so the tree that gets committed names the nodes it was generated on: both trees now hold four
Jobs called `<suite>-fill-<identity>-k3d-dev-cluster-agent-0` and the same for `server-0`. That is a
change in kind rather than degree — the tree used to carry a cache DaemonSet, which named nothing —
and it is left in place for now because the tree is generated output: the runbook regenerates both
trees at the start of every run before it applies them, and a reader of the repository sees the
shape the design produces. The owner should decide whether a _distributable_ tree may name nodes at
all. The alternatives are a `nodeSelector` on `kubernetes.io/hostname` rather than `nodeName`, which
keeps the pin but not the name; generating the fill Jobs only on the cluster-driven path and leaving
the committed tree node-free, which splits the tree in two; or ignoring the fill Job files in the
repository, which hides the very part of the design that reads best in a diff.

Answered by the split: the committed base holds no node name, and the ignored overlay holds the
per-node fill Jobs.

### D-503 — A switchable service's objects sit in the shared base

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

A `services` switch is a deploy-level fact that removes objects, but the split places those objects
in the artifact's committed base, where no deploy can remove them: `placementOf` returns `base` for
everything that is not instantiated by name or patched through the CR, so a switchable backing
service's Deployment, claim and credentials copy are applied by every deploy, switched off or not,
and the pass cannot prune what the tree still names (T-317, run 38089069133). Two fixes, and the
choice is not mine to make. Placing a switchable service's objects in the overlay, or having the
overlay instantiate them, is the principled one: anything a deployment may switch off is not
deploy-independent, so it does not belong in a shared base, and the cost is that every deploy writes
those manifests itself and the committed bases change shape. Regenerating the tree when the
declaration carries a switch - using the shipped base only when `spec.services` names nothing
switched off - is the small one: it keeps the committed bases as they are and gives up the overlay
path for switched deploys only, but it leaves a base that is semantically mixed, since it still
carries objects some deploys do not want.

Superseded by `D-504`.

### D-434 — The deployment page needs a route from the portal to the operator API

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

The operator now serves its read API on the gateway port (8080), which a browser can reach in the
cluster but not across namespaces without a route: the portal lives in the suite namespace, the
operator in blong-system, and T-258 recorded that an Ingress backend has to be a Service in its own
namespace, which is why no suite portal can front the operator directly. The page therefore needs a
decision from the user: a suite-side proxy route that forwards to the operator, an Ingress in
blong-system with its own host, or the UI reading the CRs through the suite gateway with the
operator kept out of the request path. The last is the cheapest and needs the suite to hold the read
handlers, the first keeps the operator the only reader of the cluster, and the middle exposes the
operator on a second host. Which one it is decides where authentication happens as well: the
operator verifies the same gateway keys the suite mints with, so a token from the suite login is
accepted by both.

Superseded by `D-523`.

Superseded by the confirmation the entry asked for: the install-level host, with the operator

### D-528 — Sessions need keys a realm without identity must supply

> _2026-10-11 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

Authentication against the cluster now works end to end: the issuer is named, the discovery and key
set are read with the process own service-account token, the audience is the cluster one, and the
identity dial is gone. What stops the page now is the session. The framework session step
(`identity.checkInternal`, reached from `oidc` after a token verifies) is what hands a caller its
MLE keys (`mle: {mlek, mlsk}`), and those are the keys an authenticated call is decrypted with. A
realm that answers its own login has no such session, so the client encrypts with what it was given
while the server decrypts with something else and the call fails as `Error: Decryption failed` at
`mle.ts:90` — while `login.token.create`, whose keys travel in the JWE header, keeps working, which
is the difference a reader can see. The choice is where those keys come from: the realm answering
the session check locally with this process gateway keys, the client using the bundle public keys
for authenticated calls too, or the session being established some other way. That is a decision
about a session boundary rather than a defect to patch, so it is recorded rather than chosen.

resolved by the realm's own session answer, see D-529

### D-433 — A realm-level declaration surface is needed for roles and cli intents

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

Two review items are one question, and it is the user to answer because it decides where a realm
says what it is. realmRoles should come from the realms rather than from the suite, and the cli
intent should be declared per package: both need a realm-level place to say k8s facts, and neither
has one today. The plan already prefers the realms: roles come from port.k8s.k8sRealmRole, with the
suite config only as a fallback, and the suite declares six roles that no realm repeats, so removing
the fallback without the declarations would turn companions into services and change every
deployment. The obstacle is that the value is read off a port, and some realms own no port of their
own: blong-core and blong-access contribute handlers to the shared srv.db adapter, so their realm
name never appears as a port id, and their only files that could carry an activation are the subject
handlers, which have none. Adding an activation block to a port that has none is not a safe way to
carry a k8s fact either, because an activation block is also what decides whether the port loads at
all. The candidates are a per-realm k8s config on the registry view, a realm-level k8s layer file,
or extending the layer.server.ts contract to publish realm facts rather than only layer activation;
the first is the smallest and needs the registry view to expose per-realm config beside groups and
ports. Until it is chosen, the plan keeps the suite fallback and the deployment split stays as it
is.

Implemented: the loader records each realm's own active config under its name, Registry.describe()
publishes it as realmConfig, and registryView reads k8sRealmRole from there with a port declaration
as fallback. Declarations live in each realm's own server.ts - server companion, core and access
both, blong and kustomize and the codec realm none - and the suite's realmRoles list,
IPlanOptions.realmRoles, IPlanConfig.realmRoles and the plan's fallback are gone. F-418 records the
trap the first version fell into.

Superseded by `D-437`.

### D-541 — The embedded fill module carries no comments

> _2026-10-13 · realm/blong-kustomize · superseded_

The copy of fill.ts that a fill Job runs is the module with its comments removed: stripComments in
artifact.ts scans the source and keeps every newline, and the ConfigMap carries the base64 of that
text. Two things follow. The prose that explains the code stays where it is read, in the source, and
no comment travels to a cluster. And a re-worded comment no longer rewrites the generated tree or
its snapshot, so trimming the prose of a file cannot fail a test in another package. Newlines are
kept so a stack trace from the mounted copy still names the line the source has, and the
mounted-copy case in testFill mounts the shipped bytes rather than the file. When the code itself
changes, npm run sync-derived regenerates both the install tree and the snapshots; a comment-only
change needs neither.

Superseded by `D-542`.

Replaced by a real minifier: swc writes fill.min.mts, which the ConfigMap carries and a test keeps
fresh.
